newsitem.title: USA: Advocates gear up for battle over NATO expansion.
newsitem.headline: Advocates gear up for battle over NATO expansion.

text.p: A vote in the U.S. Senate may be a year away, but advocates of NATO enlargement are mobilising now for the debate over one of America's most important post-Cold War foreign policy decisions.

President Bill Clinton, a prime mover in plans to expand the Western military alliance into eastern Europe, is taking no chances to secure essential congressional approval. A Senate test vote last year was overwhelmingly in favour of the policy, 81-16, but media criticism is growing.

This spring the Clinton administration opened a NATO Enlargement Ratification Office to promote the cause, making its director, Jeremy Rosner, an adviser to both the president and the secretary of state.

On Capitol Hill, Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott of Mississippi, a supporter of expansion, has named a bipartisan NATO Observer Group of senators to work on questions about the issue in the months before the expected vote.

"You may think this issue is a pushover. This is not a pushover because it's a serious commitment ... We have never considered the 81 votes to be solid," a senior administration official said, speaking on condition of anonymity.
Doubters of the wisdom of NATO expansion say they have many questions including the costs -- there are various estimates of the U.S. share -- and the risks.

"I would have to assume if a vote were taken now they would have the votes to go ahead. But there is going to be some time to think about it ... and there are a lot of unanswered questions," said Sen. Jeff Bingaman, a New Mexico Democrat who opposed expansion in the test vote last year but is undecided how he will vote next time the issue comes up.

Clinton began talking publicly about enlarging NATO in 1994, but last year he dramatically stepped up his efforts, making it a major foreign policy goal and setting 1999 as a target date for welcoming new members.

At a NATO summit in Madrid in July, the 16 members of NATO are expected to invite the Czech Republic, Poland, Hungary and perhaps others to join. That will launch negotiations with the invitees on "accession protocols" that would then need to be ratified by the United States and other NATO members.
The Clinton administration hopes the protocols can be submitted to the Senate around the start of next year. A two-thirds majority, or 67 votes, is needed for passage.

The decision has major implications for America's position in the world after the collapse of the Soviet Union and its old military bloc, the Warsaw Pact. Moscow opposes NATO expansion but has been partly mollified by a new NATO-Russia pact that gives it a voice in NATO affairs.

Rosner, head of the new NATO enlargement office, said he would be working with Capitol Hill, the public and the media to try to build and keep support for the idea. "Although it's the senators that cast the votes on ratification, certainly they will not do that in the absence of a supportive debate and a supportive public and a supportive House of Representatives ," he said.

Many Republicans support the policy and administration officials want to preserve that bipartisanship, not least because Congress has a Republican majority. So the administration was pleased when Lott set up the NATO observer group, and Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and her deputy, Strobe Talbott, already have met with them.
The group's co-chairs, Republican William Roth and Democrat Joe Biden, both of Delaware, travelled with Clinton to Paris last week for the signing of the new pact with Russia.
